```{python setup}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import os, sys, math
sys.path.append('.')
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Polygon as MplPolygon, Circle, FancyArrowPatch
from notes_style import (use_chapter, save, tidy, iso, iso_face,
                         INK, LOADCLR, REACTCLR, DIMCLR,
                         DOMCLR, BDRYCLR, FLUXCLR, MESHCLR, REFCLR)
IMGDIR = use_chapter("Class21")
import c21_figures as C21F      # the static figures, drawn from the widget's own geometry
TRI  = "#cfe3f5"
QUAD = "#ffe9a8"
GHOST= "#eceff3"

def solid(ax, V, faces, fcs, lw=1.4, ec=INK):
    """Convex solid drawn as an engineering sketch: shaded visible faces,
    hidden edges dashed, hidden vertices hollow.  Faces must be listed
    counter-clockwise as seen from OUTSIDE."""
    import matplotlib.colors as mc
    Lt = np.array([0.35, -0.55, 0.76]); Lt = Lt/np.linalg.norm(Lt)
    vis_faces, seen = [], set()
    for i, f in enumerate(faces):
        xy = [iso(*V[k]) for k in f]
        a = 0.0
        for j in range(len(xy)):
            x0, y0 = xy[j]; x1, y1 = xy[(j+1) % len(xy)]
            a += x0*y1 - x1*y0
        if a > 0:
            vis_faces.append(i); seen.update(f)

    # shaded faces first, with no edge of their own
    for i in vis_faces:
        f = faces[i]
        P = [np.array(V[k], float) for k in f]
        n = np.cross(P[1]-P[0], P[2]-P[0]); n = n/(np.linalg.norm(n) or 1)
        sh = 0.62 + 0.38*max(0.0, float(n @ Lt))
        rgb = np.array(mc.to_rgb(fcs[i]))
        ax.add_patch(MplPolygon([iso(*V[k]) for k in f], closed=True,
                                facecolor=tuple(1-(1-rgb)*sh),
                                edgecolor="none", zorder=3))

    # every edge, classified
    edges = {}
    for i, f in enumerate(faces):
        for j in range(len(f)):
            e = frozenset((f[j], f[(j+1) % len(f)]))
            edges[e] = edges.get(e, False) or (i in vis_faces)
    for e, visible in edges.items():
        a, b = tuple(e)
        (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = iso(*V[a]), iso(*V[b])
        if visible:
            ax.plot([x0,x1], [y0,y1], "-", color=ec, lw=lw, zorder=5,
                    solid_capstyle="round")
        else:
            ax.plot([x0,x1], [y0,y1], "--", color="0.45", lw=1.0,
                    dashes=(4,2.6), zorder=4)

    # vertices: filled if on a visible face, hollow if hidden behind the solid
    for k in range(len(V)):
        x, y = iso(*V[k])
        if k in seen:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", ms=4.8, color=INK, zorder=7)
        else:
            ax.plot(x, y, "o", ms=4.8, mfc="white", mec="0.45",
                    mew=1.2, zorder=7)
    return [iso(*v) for v in V]

def square_axes(axs, pts_list, pad=0.22):
    """Give every panel the same span, each centred on its own solid, so the
    relative sizes are honest and the captions line up."""
    span = max(max(max(x for x,_ in P)-min(x for x,_ in P),
                   max(y for _,y in P)-min(y for _,y in P)) for P in pts_list)
    for ax, P in zip(axs, pts_list):
        cx = (max(x for x,_ in P)+min(x for x,_ in P))/2
        cy = (max(y for _,y in P)+min(y for _,y in P))/2
        h = span/2 + pad
        ax.set_xlim(cx-h, cx+h); ax.set_ylim(cy-h, cy+h)

def frame(ax, title, sub=None):
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=12.5, fontweight="600", color=INK, pad=4)
    if sub: ax.text(0.5, -0.12, sub, transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center",
                    va="top", fontsize=10.5, color="0.35")
```

The a finite element method requires a basis to approximate the solution to a problem of interest.
These bases are defined using the structure of a number of cells glued together to approximate the intended shape as a *mesh*.

Meshes are typically created by pushing a computer-aided design (CAD) model through a specialized software, though sometimes they come as the result of processing geographic data or point cloud information. 
To get to a finite element mesh, somebody likely designed the part in CAD and somebody chose how to chop it up.
Both of decisions are then baked into your answer before you assemble a single element matrix. 
This class is a very brief introduction to those two steps, as well as a proposed pipeline to use a the CAD model for analysis directly without the use of an intermediary mesh.

## What a mesh is made of

For traditional FEM, mesh elements are convex triangles or quadrilaterals in two dimensions, or convex tetrahedra, pyramids, prisms, or hexahedra in three dimensions.

![Four typical volumetric finite elements are shown. 
Most meshes rely primarily on tetrahedra and hexahedra, while prisms and pyramids mostly exist so that a hexahedral region can transition to an unstructured tetrahedral region.](`{python} fig2_path`){#fig-c21-volume width=100%}

### Triangles and tetrahedra: easy to get but not always what you want

Generating a good triangular or tetrahedral mesh of an arbitrary shape is in many senses a solved problem. 
The algorithms to generate these are robust, automatic, and in some cases decades old.
You can frequently hand a tet mesher a complicated part and get a usable mesh without user intervention, even if the model itself has problems. 
Local refinement on these meshes is also easily done by splitting a single tetrahedron and patching up its neighbours.

Triangular and tetrahedral elements (together called *simplicial* elements) work well for a large class of problems.
However, they may perform poorly in some cases, such as

- **Directional physics.** In a boundary layer the solution changes dramatically across the layer and barely at all along it. 
What you want there is a stack of elements aligned *with* the wall. 
Tetrahedra lack capacity to effectively operate for these directional problems, and typically give poor results here.
- **Nonlinear and constrained problems.** Linear tetrahedra are notoriously stiff when the material is nearly incompressible or has gone plastic because there are not enough degrees of freedom per element to satisfy the constraint and still deform. 
This phenomenon is called **locking** and solutions using simplicial meshes are far too stiff compared to the actual solution without extensive mesh refinement.

### Quadrilaterals and hexahedra: better elements but worse to build

A hex mesh will generally get you a given accuracy with far fewer elements, handles directional features gracefully, and behaves much better on the nonlinear problems above.
The challenge is that **automatic all-hex meshing of a general solid is not a solved problem**.
Real hex meshes are often built with substantial manual guidance --- decomposing the part into mappable blocks by hand --- and unstructured local refinement is challenging because you cannot split one hexahedron without propagating the change through a whole layer of its neighbours.

**Prisms and pyramids are the glue.** They are rarely the point of a mesh. 
A pyramid has a quadrilateral on one face and triangles on the others, which is exactly what you need to close the gap where a hex block meets a tet region.
Prisms do the same job for extruded boundary layers sitting on top of a tet interior.

### Meshes are usually straight, recent trends are going towards curvilinear representations

```{python}
#| output: false
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.2))
th = np.linspace(0, np.pi/2, 400)
def shell(ax, n, curved, title, sub):
    tk = np.linspace(0, np.pi/2, n+1)
    for r0, r1 in [(1.0, 1.6)]:
        for i in range(n):
            if curved:
                t = np.linspace(tk[i], tk[i+1], 24)
                xs = np.concatenate([r0*np.cos(t), r1*np.cos(t[::-1])])
                ys = np.concatenate([r0*np.sin(t), r1*np.sin(t[::-1])])
            else:
                t = np.array([tk[i], tk[i+1]])
                xs = np.concatenate([r0*np.cos(t), r1*np.cos(t[::-1])])
                ys = np.concatenate([r0*np.sin(t), r1*np.sin(t[::-1])])
            ax.add_patch(MplPolygon(np.c_[xs, ys], closed=True,
                                    facecolor=QUAD, edgecolor=INK, lw=1.1))
    ax.plot(1.0*np.cos(th), 1.0*np.sin(th), color=LOADCLR, lw=1.8, ls="--", zorder=6)
    ax.plot(1.6*np.cos(th), 1.6*np.sin(th), color=LOADCLR, lw=1.8, ls="--", zorder=6)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 1.75); ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 1.75)
    frame(ax, title, sub)
shell(axs[0], 3, False, "straight-sided, coarse", "the red curve is the true boundary")
shell(axs[1], 9, False, "straight-sided, refined", "error shrinks, never vanishes")
shell(axs[2], 3, True,  "curved elements", "exact boundary, 3 elements")
fig3_path = save(fig, "C21_Fig3_Curved.png")
```

![For an identical curved geometry, meshes can be defined in a variety of ways. 
On the left, a coarse straight-sided mesh approximates geometry dramatically.
In the center, this can be reduced by additional mesh refinement with (bi-)linear elements, but the approximation is never fully removed.
However, curving the elements (on the right) fixes the geometry without adding elements, but through the use of higher polynomials.](`{python} fig3_path`){#fig-c21-curved width=100%}

Most meshes in used in industry are piecewise linear, with straight edges, and flat faces. 
This allows for a simple representation and is directly usable for all finite element methods.
However, this comes at the price of accurate geometry.
For the quarter annulus of [Class 20](20_Class.qmd), this introduced a half-percent length error through geometry error, not quadrature error, and no refinement mechanism could address it. 
**Curved (higher-order) meshes** have extra nodes per edge so the element can bend to the real boundary, and they are becoming common wherever the geometry matters, including for boundary layers, electromagnetics, and anything run at high polynomial degree, where a straight-sided boundary caps convergence rate no matter how good the basis is.

### More about mesh data structures

The above discussion describes what mesh elements are used. 
To learn more about how a mesh is actually described and how to navigate around a mesh, one should understand the half-edge data structure.
The following is a good interactive page describing how surface meshes are defined and operate: [jerryyin.info/geometry-processing-algorithms/half-edge](https://jerryyin.info/geometry-processing-algorithms/half-edge/).

## Where meshes come from

A significant number of meshes are generated from a CAD model. 
Others come from measurement instead, such as a laser
scan to produce a point cloud or a CT/MRI scan to produce voxels, both of which can be meshed. 
The CAD route is the most common one in traditional engineering design and will be discussed hereafter.
While you should be aware that you can mesh other data, we will not cover this content in this class.

A CAD model stores smooth surfaces. 
A mesh stores kinked facets.
Converting from CAD model to a mesh throws away exact geometry, which may affect both geometric and analysis precision.

### Boundary representation

CAD describes a solid by describing only describing the outside surfaces.
This is called a **boundary representation**, or B-rep, and the model is a collection of surfaces, many of which are cut in some form and then stitched together along shared edges so that they enclose a volume.
There is no description of the inside.
The solid is whatever the skin contains.
On the occasion that a CAD model does not represent the outside of a volume, it is typically representative of the solid's midsurface, and in these cases is called an *open B-rep*, whereas volume-enclosing B-reps are called *closed B-reps* or just simply *B-reps*.

Each surface of a B-rep is almost always a **B-spline** or **NURBS** surface. 
These are defined using the same kind of content learned in Class 12, where a spline surface is a mapping from a parametric square or rectangle into a curved patch in space,

$$ \underline{x}(u,v), \qquad (u,v) \in [0,1]^2 , $$

built from basis functions in $u$ times basis functions in $v$. 
(Note that here we typically use $u$ and $v$ for the parametric coordinates compared to $\xi$ and $\eta$ for the reference or parent coordinates.)
The same tensor-productconstruction as is used for bilinear and biquadratic elements, is used for B-splines and NURBS, but just using a different basis, which will be discussed further below.

An example of a B-rep is shown in the widget below.
The grey curves are **isocurves**, which are curves of constant $u$ or constant $v$ on each surface. 
They are the image of a grid in the parametric square, and they are the clearest way to see that a CAD surface is a mapped square.
Cutting operations that mask parts of the curvilinear surfaces are called trimming curves, and can be turned on or off as well.

```{=html}
<script>
(function(){
var AZ=-2.27, EL=0.28, NISO=7, ISO=true, BND=true, HOLE=true, FILL=true, EXT=false,
    WALL=true, SOLID=true, S='';
var AZ0=AZ, EL0=EL, ZM=1;   /* the starting view, and the zoom about it */
function clampZ(z){ return Math.max(0.45, Math.min(6, z)); }
var WCLR='#9fb4d0';   /* the material seen edge-on */
var INK='#18202b',GREY='#6b7684',FAINT='#dfe4ea',ACC='#b8322a',BLUE='#2b5fa8',VIO='#6d28d9';

/* ---- the bracket: five CURVED trimmed patches ----
   Cross-section, walking across the part:  flange - fillet - web - fillet -
   flange.  The web is the flat plate joining the two naked fillet edges; each
   flange leaves its fillet tangentially and carries a hole.  Nothing is
   planar except the web, and the trim curves live in the parametric domain,
   which is where CAD keeps them.                                        */
var THETA=90*Math.PI/180, RF=0.40, HW=0.62, LF=1.75;
var BLO=0.10, BHI=0.90;   /* the band kept on the web, fillets and flange roots */
var ZB0=-0.12, ZT0=2.20;

/* the common seam heights, so neighbouring patches meet exactly */
function zbF(u){ return ZB0 - 0.38*u; }
function ztF(u){ return ZT0 - 0.50*u - 0.30*u*u; }

/* where a fillet starts and ends, in the cross-section plane */
function filletCtr(sgn){ return [RF, sgn*HW]; }
function filletEnd(sgn){
  return [RF*(1-Math.cos(THETA)), sgn*(HW + RF*Math.sin(THETA))];
}
function flangeDir(sgn){ return [Math.sin(THETA), sgn*Math.cos(THETA)]; }

/* 1. the web: the flat plate between the two naked fillet edges */
var WEB={ kind:'web', hole:null, vlo:BLO, vhi:BHI, ref:[1,0,0],
  seams:['u0','u1'],
  pt:function(u,v){
    var y=-HW + 2*HW*u;
    return [0, y, ZB0 + v*(ZT0-ZB0)];   /* straight top and bottom edges */
  }};

/* 2. the fillets: cylindrical strips turning the web into each flange */
function fillet(sgn){
  return { kind:'fillet', hole:null, vlo:BLO, vhi:BHI, seams:['u0','u1'],
    ref:[Math.SQRT1_2, -sgn*Math.SQRT1_2, 0],
    pt:function(u,v){
      var c=filletCtr(sgn), ph=Math.PI - THETA*u;
      var x=c[0]+RF*Math.cos(ph), y=c[1]+sgn*RF*Math.sin(ph);
      return [x, y, ZB0+v*(ZT0-ZB0)];
    }};
}
/* 3. the flanges: tangent to the fillet, tapering, each with a hole */
function flange(sgn){
  return { kind:'flange', ref:[0,-sgn,0], seams:['u0'],
    pt:function(u,v){
      var e=filletEnd(sgn), d=flangeDir(sgn), L=LF*u;
      return [e[0]+L*d[0], e[1]+L*d[1], zbF(u)+v*(ztF(u)-zbF(u))];
    },
    hole:{uc:0.50, vc:0.45, ru:0.20, rv:0.18},
    /* near the seam the flange keeps only the same band as the fillet, so the
       top and bottom trim curves run straight through the join; past u0 it
       opens out to full height.  The two steps are the orthogonal corners. */
    step:{u0:0.28, vlo:BLO, vhi:BHI},
    /* the two outer corners are cut off on the diagonal */
    tri:{a:0.26, b:0.30}
  };
}
var MID=[flange(1), fillet(1), WEB, fillet(-1), flange(-1)];

/* The bracket is a thin part, so the solid is bounded by two surfaces: the
   mid-surface pushed out by half the thickness and pulled in by half.  Each
   patch's unit normal comes from its own two parametric tangents, with the
   sign settled by the patch's `ref` so that "in" means the same thing on all
   five.  The parametric square, and therefore every trim drawn in it, is
   shared by the two offsets -- only the mapping into space differs. */
var TH=0.13;
function nrmOf(p,u,v){
  var e=1e-4,
      uu=Math.min(Math.max(u,e),1-e), vv=Math.min(Math.max(v,e),1-e),
      a=p.pt(uu+e,vv), b=p.pt(uu-e,vv), c=p.pt(uu,vv+e), d=p.pt(uu,vv-e),
      tu=[a[0]-b[0],a[1]-b[1],a[2]-b[2]],
      tv=[c[0]-d[0],c[1]-d[1],c[2]-d[2]],
      n=[tu[1]*tv[2]-tu[2]*tv[1], tu[2]*tv[0]-tu[0]*tv[2], tu[0]*tv[1]-tu[1]*tv[0]],
      L=Math.sqrt(n[0]*n[0]+n[1]*n[1]+n[2]*n[2])||1, r=p.ref, k;
  n=[n[0]/L,n[1]/L,n[2]/L];
  if(n[0]*r[0]+n[1]*r[1]+n[2]*r[2]<0) n=[-n[0],-n[1],-n[2]];
  return n;
}
function offsetOf(base,s){
  var o={}, k; for(k in base) o[k]=base[k];
  o.side=s;
  o.pt=function(u,v){
    var q=base.pt(u,v), n=nrmOf(base,u,v), t=s*TH*0.5;
    return [q[0]+t*n[0], q[1]+t*n[1], q[2]+t*n[2]];
  };
  return o;
}
var OUTER=MID.map(function(b){return offsetOf(b,-1);}),  /* the larger shell */
    INNER=MID.map(function(b){return offsetOf(b,+1);});  /* the smaller one  */
var PANELS=OUTER.concat(INNER);

/* ---- the side walls ---------------------------------------------------
   The two offsets are only the faces of the material.  Every edge of the
   trimmed region that is NOT shared with a neighbouring patch is an exposed
   edge of the solid, and the material there is closed off by a ruled surface
   running from the outer face to the inner one.  Each hole closes the same
   way, which makes a cylinder.  Seam edges get no wall: the material runs
   straight through a seam, which is what makes the five patches one part. */
function offAt(base,u,v,s){
  var q=base.pt(u,v), n=nrmOf(base,u,v), t=s*TH*0.5;
  return [q[0]+t*n[0], q[1]+t*n[1], q[2]+t*n[2]];
}
function isSeamSeg(p,sg){
  var S=p.seams||[], e=1e-9;
  if(Math.abs(sg.a[0])  <e && Math.abs(sg.b[0])  <e) return S.indexOf('u0')>=0;
  if(Math.abs(sg.a[0]-1)<e && Math.abs(sg.b[0]-1)<e) return S.indexOf('u1')>=0;
  return false;
}
function wall(base,crv,kind){
  var W={ kind:kind, base:base,
    pt:function(t,w){ var c=crv(t); return offAt(base,c[0],c[1],-1+2*w); } };
  /* how long this wall is, so its grid can be spaced like everyone else's */
  var L=0, k, a=W.pt(0,0.5), b;
  for(k=1;k<=24;k++){
    b=W.pt(k/24,0.5);
    L+=Math.sqrt((b[0]-a[0])*(b[0]-a[0])+(b[1]-a[1])*(b[1]-a[1])+(b[2]-a[2])*(b[2]-a[2]));
    a=b;
  }
  W.span=L;
  return W;
}
function lineCrv(a,b){
  return function(t){ return [a[0]+(b[0]-a[0])*t, a[1]+(b[1]-a[1])*t]; };
}
function holeCrv(h){
  return function(t){ var th=2*Math.PI*t;
    return [h.uc+h.ru*Math.cos(th), h.vc+h.rv*Math.sin(th)]; };
}
var WALLS=(function(){
  var W=[],i,j;
  for(i=0;i<MID.length;i++){
    var p=MID[i], sg=regionSegs(p);
    for(j=0;j<sg.length;j++)
      if(!isSeamSeg(p,sg[j])) W.push(wall(p, lineCrv(sg[j].a, sg[j].b), 'wall'));
    if(p.hole) W.push(wall(p, holeCrv(p.hole), 'bore'));
  }
  return W;
})();
function wallLoop(W,n){
  var P=[],k;
  for(k=0;k<=n;k++) P.push(W.pt(k/n,0));
  for(k=n;k>=0;k--) P.push(W.pt(k/n,1));
  return P;
}
/* An isocurve on a wall.  A wall carries no trim of its own, so there is
   nothing to split: fixT holds t and runs across the thickness (a straight
   ruling), otherwise w is held and the curve runs along the edge. */
function wallIso(W,fixT,val,n){
  var P=[],k;
  for(k=0;k<=n;k++){ var t=k/n; P.push(fixT ? W.pt(val,t) : W.pt(t,val)); }
  return P;
}
/* A bore is a closed tube, so its two rims are separate loops and the band
   between them is the even-odd difference of the two. */
function wallPath(W){
  if(W.kind!=='bore') return path(wallLoop(W,24),true);
  var a=[],b=[],k;
  for(k=0;k<=48;k++){ a.push(W.pt(k/48,0)); b.push(W.pt(k/48,1)); }
  return path(a,true)+' '+path(b,true);
}

/* Keep the geometry in one place.  Any later view of this bracket should
   read this object rather than define a second, almost-the-same bracket. */
window.C21Bracket={panels:PANELS, mid:MID, outer:OUTER, inner:INNER, walls:WALLS,
                   flange:flange, fillet:fillet, web:WEB, thickness:TH};

function at(p,u,v){ return p.pt(u,v); }
function VLO(p){ return p.vlo===undefined?0:p.vlo; }
function VHI(p){ return p.vhi===undefined?1:p.vhi; }

/* Everything a CAD trim can do here, tested in the PARAMETRIC domain:
   a band off the top and bottom, an orthogonal corner notch, and a hole. */
function clipped(p,u,v){
  if(p.step){
    if(u<p.step.u0 && (v<p.step.vlo-1e-9 || v>p.step.vhi+1e-9)) return true;
  } else if(v<VLO(p)-1e-9 || v>VHI(p)+1e-9) return true;
  if(p.tri){
    var ta=p.tri.a, tb=p.tri.b;
    /* bottom-outer corner: chord (1-a,0) -> (1,b) */
    if(tb*(u-1+ta) - ta*v > 0) return true;
    /* top-outer corner:    chord (1-a,1) -> (1,1-b) */
    if(tb*(u-1+ta) + ta*(v-1) > 0) return true;
  }
  if(p.hole){
    var a=(u-p.hole.uc)/p.hole.ru, b=(v-p.hole.vc)/p.hole.rv;
    if(a*a+b*b<1) return true;
  }
  return false;
}
function holeLoop(p,n){
  if(!p.hole) return [];
  var o=[];
  for(var k=0;k<=n;k++){ var t=2*Math.PI*k/n;
    o.push(p.pt(p.hole.uc+p.hole.ru*Math.cos(t), p.hole.vc+p.hole.rv*Math.sin(t))); }
  return o;
}
/* the boundary of the kept region, in parameter space, each piece tagged
   'bnd' where it is a natural edge of the patch and 'trim' where a trim
   curve cuts into it */
function regionSegs(p){
  var S=[];
  function seg(a,b,t){ S.push({a:a,b:b,t:t}); }
  if(p.step){
    var u0=p.step.u0, lo=p.step.vlo, hi=p.step.vhi;
    seg([0,lo],[u0,lo],'trim');      /* continues the fillet's bottom trim   */
    seg([u0,lo],[u0,0],'trim');      /* the orthogonal corner, going down    */
    if(p.tri){
      var ta=p.tri.a, tb=p.tri.b;
      seg([u0,0],[1-ta,0],'bnd');
      seg([1-ta,0],[1,tb],'trim');          /* bottom-outer chamfer */
      seg([1,tb],[1,1-tb],'bnd');
      seg([1,1-tb],[1-ta,1],'trim');        /* top-outer chamfer    */
      seg([1-ta,1],[u0,1],'bnd');
    } else {
      seg([u0,0],[1,0],'bnd');
      seg([1,0],[1,1],'bnd');
      seg([1,1],[u0,1],'bnd');
    }
    seg([u0,1],[u0,hi],'trim');      /* the orthogonal corner, coming back   */
    seg([u0,hi],[0,hi],'trim');      /* continues the fillet's top trim      */
    seg([0,hi],[0,lo],'bnd');
  } else {
    var a=VLO(p), b=VHI(p);
    seg([0,a],[1,a], a>0?'trim':'bnd');
    seg([1,a],[1,b], 'bnd');
    seg([1,b],[0,b], b<1?'trim':'bnd');
    seg([0,b],[0,a], 'bnd');
  }
  return S;
}
function segPts(p,sg,n){
  var o=[];
  for(var k=0;k<=n;k++){ var t=k/n;
    o.push(p.pt(sg.a[0]+(sg.b[0]-sg.a[0])*t, sg.a[1]+(sg.b[1]-sg.a[1])*t)); }
  return o;
}
function regionLoop(p,n){
  var sg=regionSegs(p), o=[];
  for(var i=0;i<sg.length;i++){
    var q=segPts(p,sg[i],n);
    for(var k=(i?1:0);k<q.length;k++) o.push(q[k]);
  }
  return o;
}
/* ---- camera ---- */
function rot(q){
  var ca=Math.cos(AZ),sa=Math.sin(AZ),ce=Math.cos(EL),se=Math.sin(EL);
  var x=ca*q[0]-sa*q[1], y=sa*q[0]+ca*q[1], z=q[2];
  return [x, ce*y-se*z, se*y+ce*z];
}
/* Fit once, from the object's bounding sphere, so it never clips or jumps
   while you drag. */
var CX=440, CY=238, SC=104, CEN=[0,0,0];
(function(){
  var pts=[],i,k;
  for(i=0;i<PANELS.length;i++){
    var p=PANELS[i];
    for(var a=0;a<=4;a++) for(var b=0;b<=4;b++) pts.push(p.pt(a/4,b/4));
    var h=holeLoop(p,16); for(k=0;k<h.length;k++) pts.push(h[k]);
  }
  var c=[0,0,0];
  for(i=0;i<pts.length;i++) for(k=0;k<3;k++) c[k]+=pts[i][k]/pts.length;
  CEN=c;
  var R=0;
  for(i=0;i<pts.length;i++){
    var dx=pts[i][0]-c[0],dy=pts[i][1]-c[1],dz=pts[i][2]-c[2];
    R=Math.max(R,Math.sqrt(dx*dx+dy*dy+dz*dz));
  }
  SC=214/R;                                   /* fills the frame, fits at any orientation */
})();
function proj(q){
  var r=rot([q[0]-CEN[0], q[1]-CEN[1], q[2]-CEN[2]]), k=SC*ZM;
  return [CX+k*r[0], CY-k*r[2]];
}
function depth(q){ return rot([q[0]-CEN[0],q[1]-CEN[1],q[2]-CEN[2]])[1]; }

function path(pts,close){
  var d='';
  for(var i=0;i<pts.length;i++){var q=proj(pts[i]); d+=(i?' L':'M')+q[0].toFixed(1)+' '+q[1].toFixed(1);}
  return d+(close?'Z':'');
}
/* An isocurve, split into the part the trim keeps and the part it removes.
   The removed part is still on the surface -- that is the whole point of a
   trim -- so the widget can draw it faintly on request. */
function isoCurve(p,fixU,val,n){
  var keep=[],drop=[],cur=[],curDrop=null;
  for(var k=0;k<=n;k++){
    var t=k/n, u=fixU?val:t, v=fixU?t:val, off=clipped(p,u,v), q=p.pt(u,v);
    if(off===curDrop){ cur.push(q); }
    else {
      if(cur.length>1) (curDrop?drop:keep).push(cur);
      cur=[q]; curDrop=off;
    }
  }
  if(cur.length>1) (curDrop?drop:keep).push(cur);
  return {keep:keep, drop:drop};
}

function draw(){
  S='';
  // back-to-front by patch centroid depth
  /* closed: both offsets and the walls between them.  open: the mid-surface
     on its own, which is the shell the two offsets were made from. */
  var PL=SOLID?PANELS:MID, WL=SOLID?WALLS:[];
  var NP=PL.length, oi;
  function cenOf(i){ return i<NP ? at(PL[i],0.5,0.5) : WL[i-NP].pt(0.5,0.5); }
  var order=[]; for(oi=0;oi<NP+WL.length;oi++) order.push(oi);
  order.sort(function(a,b){ return depth(cenOf(b))-depth(cenOf(a)); });
  for(oi=0;oi<order.length;oi++){
    if(order[oi]>=NP){                         /* a side wall or a bore */
      if(WALL){
        var W=WL[order[oi]-NP], bore=(W.kind==='bore'), nt=bore?48:24, wi;
        if(FILL)
          S+='<path d="'+wallPath(W)+'" fill="'+WCLR+'" fill-rule="evenodd" '+
             'opacity=".72" stroke="none"/>';
        if(ISO){
          /* A wall gets the same grid as every other patch, but spaced rather
             than counted: NISO curves across a wall only a tenth as wide as it
             is long would collapse into a solid band and the surface would
             still look filled with the fill switched off.  Matching the
             spacing to the face grid keeps the cells roughly square. */
          var nw=Math.max(2, Math.min(NISO, Math.round(NISO*TH/W.span)));
          for(wi=1;wi<nw;wi++)
            S+='<path d="'+path(wallIso(W,false,wi/nw,nt),false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+
               GREY+'" stroke-width="1" opacity=".75"/>';
          for(wi=1;wi<NISO;wi++)
            S+='<path d="'+path(wallIso(W,true,wi/NISO,2),false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+
               GREY+'" stroke-width="1" opacity=".75"/>';
        }
        /* the end rulings, where this wall meets the next one round */
        if(BND && !bore)
          for(wi=0;wi<2;wi++)
            S+='<path d="'+path(wallIso(W,true,wi,2),false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+
               VIO+'" stroke-width="1.6" opacity=".85"/>';
      }
      continue;
    }
    var p=PL[order[oi]];
    if(FILL){
      // the patch, with the hole punched out using the even-odd rule
      var d=path(regionLoop(p,16),true)+(p.hole?' '+path(holeLoop(p,48),true):'');
      S+='<path d="'+d+'" fill="#dce6f2" fill-rule="evenodd" opacity=".80" stroke="none"/>';
    }
    if(ISO){
      for(var i=1;i<NISO;i++){
        var t=i/NISO, cs=[isoCurve(p,true,t,70), isoCurve(p,false,t,70)], ci, sgp;
        for(ci=0;ci<2;ci++){
          for(sgp=0;sgp<cs[ci].keep.length;sgp++)
            S+='<path d="'+path(cs[ci].keep[sgp],false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+GREY+
               '" stroke-width="1" opacity=".75"/>';
          if(EXT) for(sgp=0;sgp<cs[ci].drop.length;sgp++)
            S+='<path d="'+path(cs[ci].drop[sgp],false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+GREY+
               '" stroke-width=".9" opacity=".38" stroke-dasharray="3 3"/>';
        }
      }
    }
    /* The four natural patch edges, in blue.  A trim masks the edge of a patch
       exactly as it masks the patch itself, so each edge is split by the same
       test the isocurves use: the surviving pieces are solid, and the pieces
       the trim removed are available faintly under the same toggle. */
    if(BND){
      var ed=[isoCurve(p,true,0,60), isoCurve(p,true,1,60),
              isoCurve(p,false,0,60), isoCurve(p,false,1,60)], ei, ep;
      for(ei=0;ei<4;ei++){
        for(ep=0;ep<ed[ei].keep.length;ep++)
          S+='<path d="'+path(ed[ei].keep[ep],false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+BLUE+
             '" stroke-width="2.4"/>';
        if(EXT) for(ep=0;ep<ed[ei].drop.length;ep++)
          S+='<path d="'+path(ed[ei].drop[ep],false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+BLUE+
             '" stroke-width="1.7" opacity=".62" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/>';
      }
    }
    /* trim curves in red */
    if(HOLE){
      var sg=regionSegs(p);
      for(var qi=0;qi<sg.length;qi++){
        if(sg[qi].t!=='trim') continue;
        S+='<path d="'+path(segPts(p,sg[qi],16),false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+ACC+
           '" stroke-width="2.2"/>';
      }
    }
    if(HOLE && p.hole)
      S+='<path d="'+path(holeLoop(p,64),true)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+ACC+
         '" stroke-width="2.4"/>';
  }
  /* The seams where neighbouring patches are stitched together.  A seam is
     the shared boundary of two patches, so it answers to the same switch as
     the free boundaries do -- as the wall rulings already did. */
  if(BND){
    var seams=(SOLID?[0,1,3,4,5,6,8,9]:[0,1,3,4]).map(
          function(i){ return [PL[i], 0]; });
    for(var si=0; si<seams.length; si++){
      var sc=isoCurve(seams[si][0],true,seams[si][1],48), sp2;
      for(sp2=0;sp2<sc.keep.length;sp2++)
        S+='<path d="'+path(sc.keep[sp2],false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+VIO+
           '" stroke-width="2.6"/>';
      if(EXT) for(sp2=0;sp2<sc.drop.length;sp2++)
        S+='<path d="'+path(sc.drop[sp2],false)+'" fill="none" stroke="'+VIO+
           '" stroke-width="1.7" opacity=".62" stroke-dasharray="5 3"/>';
    }
    var ft=proj(PL[2].pt(0.5,1));
    S+='<line x1="'+ft[0]+'" y1="'+ft[1]+'" x2="'+(ft[0]+30)+'" y2="'+(ft[1]-58)+
       '" stroke="'+VIO+'" stroke-width=".9" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/>';
    S+='<text x="'+(ft[0]+34)+'" y="'+(ft[1]-58)+'" font-size="11.5" fill="'+VIO+
       '" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-weight="600">shared edges</text>';
  }
  var lx=22,ly=424;
  function key(x,col,txt,w){
    S+='<line x1="'+x+'" y1="'+ly+'" x2="'+(x+26)+'" y2="'+ly+'" stroke="'+col+
       '" stroke-width="'+(w||2.4)+'"/>'+
       '<text x="'+(x+32)+'" y="'+(ly+4)+'" font-size="11.5" fill="'+GREY+
       '" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif">'+txt+'</text>';
  }
  key(lx,GREY,'isocurves (constant u or v)',1);
  key(lx+210,BLUE,'surface boundary');
  key(lx+380,ACC,'trim curve');
  key(lx+520,VIO,'shared edges');
  document.getElementById('brk').innerHTML=S;
  document.getElementById('brkcap').innerHTML=
    '<b>A closed B-rep of a bracket.</b> Each surface is a B-spline surface mapped from a '+
    'parametric square, as shown by its grey isocurves. The outer and inner faces of the bracket '+
    'are each made of five surfaces (two flanges, two fillets, and a web), and they are connected '+
    'along their edges by 24 planar side walls and by a cylinder through each hole, for 36 surfaces '+
    'in total. Red curves are trimming curves, which remove parts of a surface, such as the holes '+
    'and the chamfered corners. Blue curves are the remaining untrimmed edges of each surface, and '+
    'violet curves are the edges shared by neighbouring surfaces. Unchecking <i>closed solid</i> '+
    'shows the open B-rep of the midsurface, which has only five surfaces.';
}

/* ---- drag to rotate ---- */
var svg=document.getElementById('brk'), drag=null, pinch=null;
function pt(e){ return e.touches? {x:e.touches[0].clientX,y:e.touches[0].clientY}
                                : {x:e.clientX,y:e.clientY}; }
function gap(e){ var a=e.touches[0], b=e.touches[1];
  return Math.sqrt((a.clientX-b.clientX)*(a.clientX-b.clientX)+
                   (a.clientY-b.clientY)*(a.clientY-b.clientY)); }
function down(e){
  if(e.touches && e.touches.length===2){   /* two fingers pinch instead of turn */
    pinch={d:gap(e), z:ZM}; drag=null; e.preventDefault(); return;
  }
  drag=pt(e); svg.classList.add('drag');
}
function move(e){
  if(pinch && e.touches && e.touches.length===2){
    ZM=clampZ(pinch.z*gap(e)/pinch.d); draw(); e.preventDefault(); return;
  }
  if(!drag) return;
  var q=pt(e);
  AZ+=(q.x-drag.x)*0.010;
  EL=Math.max(-1.25,Math.min(1.25,EL+(q.y-drag.y)*0.008));
  drag=q; draw(); e.preventDefault();
}
function up(){ drag=null; pinch=null; svg.classList.remove('drag'); }
svg.addEventListener('mousedown',down); window.addEventListener('mousemove',move);
window.addEventListener('mouseup',up);
svg.addEventListener('wheel',function(e){
  ZM=clampZ(ZM*Math.exp(-e.deltaY*0.0016)); draw(); e.preventDefault();
},{passive:false});
svg.addEventListener('touchstart',down,{passive:false});
svg.addEventListener('touchmove',move,{passive:false});
window.addEventListener('touchend',up);
document.getElementById('k_iso').addEventListener('change',function(){ISO=this.checked;draw();});
document.getElementById('k_bnd').addEventListener('change',function(){BND=this.checked;draw();});
document.getElementById('k_hole').addEventListener('change',function(){HOLE=this.checked;draw();});
document.getElementById('k_fill').addEventListener('change',function(){FILL=this.checked;draw();});
document.getElementById('k_solid').addEventListener('change',function(){SOLID=this.checked;draw();});
document.getElementById('k_wall').addEventListener('change',function(){WALL=this.checked;draw();});
document.getElementById('k_ext').addEventListener('change',function(){EXT=this.checked;draw();});
document.getElementById('k_n').addEventListener('input',function(){NISO=+this.value;draw();});
document.getElementById('k_home').addEventListener('click',function(){
  AZ=AZ0; EL=EL0; ZM=1; draw(); });
draw();
})();
</script>
```

### Gluing and trimming

Very few shapes of interest can be described by a single mapped square.
The midsurface of the bracket above, for example, is built from five surfaces: a web, two fillets, and two flanges.
CAD builds shapes like this from simpler surfaces using two operations, called gluing and trimming.

**Gluing** joins surfaces along shared edges.
The violet curves in the widget mark the edges where one surface stops and the next one starts.
Gluing records that the two edges are the same curve in space, so the model has no gap there.
It can also record how smoothly the surfaces meet.
In the bracket, for example, each fillet joins the web and its flange without a corner.

**Trimming** removes part of a surface.
The designer draws a closed curve in the parametric domain of the surface, and only the part of the surface inside that curve is kept in the model.
Every red curve in the widget is a trimming curve, including the bands removed from the top and bottom, the steps and chamfered corners on the flanges, and the holes.
A hole is the simplest case.
The surface is not rebuilt with a hole in it; instead, an ellipse is drawn in its parametric domain, and everything inside the ellipse is ignored.

Trimming does not delete any of the underlying surface.
Checking *isocurves into the trimmed parts* in the widget shows the rest of each surface continuing underneath the trimmed regions.
@fig-c21-trimming takes one face out of the bracket to show the full surface from which it was cut.

```{python}
#| output: false
fig, _ = C21F.trimming_figure()
fig_trim_path = save(fig, "C21_Fig4_Trimming.png")
```

![One flange of the bracket, shown three ways. (a) The face as it appears in the model, with the rest of the bracket ghosted. (b) The untrimmed surface from which the face was cut, which is the image of the full parametric square, with the trimmed face drawn on top. The dashed blue outline and the dashed isocurves belong to the surface but not to the model. (c) The same face in its parametric domain $(u,v)$, which is where the trimming curves are stored. The arrows mark the same corner and the same two directions in (b) and (c); note that in the 3D view, $u$ runs from right to left. The violet edge is where this flange is glued to its fillet.](`{python} fig_trim_path`){#fig-c21-trimming width=100%}

Nearly every CAD model is built in this way: a collection of tensor-product surfaces, each trimmed by curves in its own parametric domain, and glued to its neighbours along shared edges.
This is an effective way to describe a shape, but it is difficult to use directly for analysis, as described next.

### Why trimming complicates analysis

Suppose we tried to perform an analysis directly on the face in panel (c) of @fig-c21-trimming, using the grid of its parametric domain as our elements.
The cells of that grid are squares, but the trimming curves do not follow the cell edges, and instead cut directly through them.

```{python}
#| output: false
fig, cut = C21F.cut_cell_figure()
fig_cut_path = save(fig, "C21_Fig5_CutCells.png")
cut_n, cut_whole = str(cut['ncut']), str(cut['ncells'] - cut['ncut'] - cut['nout'])
cut_corner = f"{cut['corner_pct']:.2f}"
cut_lost = str(9 - cut['gauss_in'])
```

![(a) The parametric domain of the flange, divided into the 7 × 7 cells between its isocurves. Each cell is shaded by the material it actually contains. Of the 49 cells, `{python} cut_n` are cut by a trimming curve (orange outline) and only `{python} cut_whole` are kept whole. The two cells at the outer corners each contain only `{python} cut_corner`% material, since the chamfer passes just inside their inner corners. (b) The cell outlined in (a), enlarged. A 3 × 3 Gauss rule built for the whole cell places `{python} cut_lost` of its 9 points inside the hole.](`{python} fig_cut_path`){#fig-c21-cutcells width=94%}

Each of the resulting problems relates to content from earlier in the course:

1. **Integration.** The Gauss rules of Classes 10 and 20 integrate over a whole element.
   On a cut cell, part of the square is not material, and the part that is has a curved boundary.
   In panel (b), a third of the quadrature points fall inside the hole.
   A cut cell requires an integration rule built for its own shape, and constructing one for every cut cell is a significant amount of work.
2. **Slivers.** A basis function whose support lies almost entirely in the trimmed region still has an unknown attached to it, even though it touches very little material, as in the corner cells.
   Its diagonal entry in the stiffness matrix is nearly zero compared with those of its neighbours, and the system of equations becomes poorly conditioned.
3. **Boundary conditions.** In Classes 14 and 19, boundary conditions were assigned to the nodes and element edges lying on $\Gamma_g$ or $\Gamma_h$.
   Here the boundary of the part is the trimming curve, which runs through the middle of cells, so there are no nodes on it to which a boundary condition can be assigned.
4. **Seams that do not quite meet.** Two glued faces each have their own trimming curve along the shared edge.
   These curves approximate the same edge in space but are generally not identical, so real models have small gaps and overlaps along their seams that a solver must tolerate.

### Meshing the bracket

The usual alternative is to mesh the CAD surfaces rather than compute on them directly.
A mesher works on the *trimmed* face, that is, on the part itself rather than on the square from which it was cut.
Every element therefore lies inside the material, and every boundary is made up of element edges.

```{python}
#| output: false
fig, msh = C21F.bracket_mesh_figure()
fig_mesh_path = save(fig, "C21_Fig6_BracketMesh.png")
mesh_quadpct = f"{msh['flange_quad_pct']:.0f}"
mesh_sides, mesh_hole = str(msh['hole_sides']), f"{msh['hole_loss_pct']:.1f}"
mesh_facets, mesh_sag = str(msh['fillet_facets']), f"{msh['fillet_sag_pct']:.1f}"
```

![(a) A quad-dominant mesh of the midsurface of the bracket, which is the surface used by a shell analysis (the *closed solid* checkbox in the widget switches between this surface and the solid). The web and the fillets are bands of their parametric domains and use a structured grid. Each flange was triangulated, neighbouring triangles were then paired into quadrilaterals wherever the pair formed a well-shaped element, and the result was smoothed; quadrilaterals cover about `{python} mesh_quadpct`% of the area of each flange. (b) The front flange laid flat, with the true boundary of the CAD face shown in red over the mesh. The hole is now a `{python} mesh_sides`-sided polygon with `{python} mesh_hole`% less area than the actual hole. Similarly, each fillet in (a) is now `{python} mesh_facets` flat strips, whose midpoints lie `{python} mesh_sag`% of the fillet radius inside the true arc.](`{python} fig_mesh_path`){#fig-c21-bracketmesh width=100%}

The four problems above no longer apply to this mesh.
There are no cut cells or slivers, the boundary is again made up of element edges, and neighbouring faces share their nodes along each seam.
The cost is the one described at the earlier in the reading, that the mesh is piecewise linear, so every curve has been replaced by straight segments.
This geometry error does not decrease with better quadrature, and is only reduced by using smaller elements or curved elements.
For many analyses of this bracket, an error of a few percent at the hole is acceptable.
For the stress at the edge of that hole, which is where the stress is largest, it may not be.

### An all-quadrilateral mesh of the same bracket

Many analysts prefer meshes without any triangles.
Some element formulations exist only for quadrilaterals, and rows of quadrilaterals that follow the edges of a part are well suited to resolving behavior along those edges.
Automatic all-quadrilateral meshing methods, such as *paving*, aim to produce these meshes by placing a row of quadrilaterals along every boundary and continuing inward until the rows meet.
A depiction of such a quadrilateral mesh is shown below.
Mesh smoothing operations are sometimes improve the quality of an initial output mesh.

<!-- This flange is a difficult case for that approach.
The hole is less than two element widths from the inside corner of the notch, so a row placed along the outer edge and a row placed around the hole would overlap almost immediately.
The outer edge is also about three times as long as the hole, so the rows cannot simply be matched one to one.
The mesh below was instead laid out by hand, in the way that an analyst might guide such a mesher.
A ring of quadrilaterals surrounds the hole, and its four outer corners are connected to the corners of the flange.
Rows of blocks follow every edge, and each chamfered corner is filled with the standard three-block pattern for a triangle.
The web and fillets use the same structured bands as before, so the two bracket meshes differ only in their flanges.

Both flanges were smoothed in the same way.
First, every node was moved to reduce the total distortion of the mesh, with boundary nodes allowed to slide along their edges and around the hole (the corners, and the seam shared with the fillet, were held fixed).
Then each interior node was moved to the position that gives the best worst-shaped element around it.
-->

```{python}
#| output: false
fig, qo = C21F.quad_only_mesh_figure()
fig_qo_path = save(fig, "C21_Fig6b_QuadOnly.png")
qo_n, qo_v5, qo_v3 = str(qo['nquad']), str(qo['valence'].get(5, 0)), str(qo['valence'].get(3, 0))
```

![(a) The midsurface of the bracket meshed with quadrilaterals only, using `{python} qo_n` elements. Rows follow every edge, including the seams shared with the fillets. (b) The front flange laid flat.  Only `{python} str(int(qo_v5)+int(qo_v3))` vertices inside the flange are irregular: `{python} qo_v5` of valence 5 at the corners of the ring, and `{python} qo_v3` of valence 3 at the centers of the corner fills.](`{python} fig_qo_path`){#fig-c21-quadonly width=100%}

### Comparing the two meshes

Mesh quality is usually measured element by element, using a few simple measures of shape and size.
The **scaled Jacobian** is found by evaluating the determinant of the Jacobian (Class 13) at each corner of an element, dividing it by the lengths of the two edges that meet there, and keeping the smallest value.
It is scaled to equal 1 for a square or an equilateral triangle, and it decreases toward 0 as the corners of the element become more distorted.
The **edge ratio** is the length of the longest edge of an element divided by the length of its shortest edge, and the **size ratio** is the area of the largest element in the mesh divided by the area of the smallest.
Both equal 1 in an ideal mesh.

```{python}
#| output: false
fig, cmp_ = C21F.mesh_quality_figure()
fig_cmp_path = save(fig, "C21_Fig6c_Quality.png")
qd_, qo_ = cmp_['qd'], cmp_['qo']
f2 = lambda x: f"{x:.2f}"; f1 = lambda x: f"{x:.1f}"; pc = lambda x: f"{x:.0f}%"
```

![The elements of each flange shaded by their scaled Jacobian: (a) the quad-dominant flange of @fig-c21-bracketmesh and (b) the quad-only flange of @fig-c21-quadonly. Darker elements are further from ideal. Both flanges use the same scale and are drawn in the same orientation as in the figures above.](`{python} fig_cmp_path`){#fig-c21-quality width=88%}

|                                                  | quad-dominant | quad-only |
|:-------------------------------------------------|--------------:|----------:|
| elements in the bracket                          | `{python} str(qd_['bracket'])` | `{python} str(qo_['bracket'])` |
| of which triangles                               | `{python} str(qd_['tris'])` | `{python} str(qo_['tris'])` |
| irregular vertices inside one flange             | `{python} str(qd_['irregular'])` | `{python} str(qo_['irregular'])` |
| scaled Jacobian of the worst element             | `{python} f2(qd_['sj_min'])` | `{python} f2(qo_['sj_min'])` |
| average scaled Jacobian                          | `{python} f2(qd_['sj_mean'])` | `{python} f2(qo_['sj_mean'])` |
| elements below 0.85                              | `{python} pc(qd_['below'])` | `{python} pc(qo_['below'])` |
| largest edge ratio in one element                | `{python} f1(qd_['er_max'])` | `{python} f1(qo_['er_max'])` |
| largest element's area ÷ smallest                | `{python} f1(qd_['size_ratio'])` | `{python} f1(qo_['size_ratio'])` |

: Both flanges measured in the same way. A vertex is irregular if other than four edges meet there. {#tbl-c21-quality}

By these shape measures, the two flanges are very similar.
Their average element quality is the same, and the automatic quad-dominant mesh has a slightly better worst element and more uniform element sizes.
This is worth noting, since an all-quadrilateral mesh is not by itself a guarantee of higher quality.
However, use of triangles for certain kinds of analyses may be strongly discouraged.

The weaker elements of the quad-only mesh are all located in the upper chamfered corner, where the ring around the hole passes close to the chamfer and the three-block fill must fit into a long, thin triangle.
Elsewhere, its elements are as good as or better than those of the quad-dominant mesh.
Its smallest elements are in the ring around the hole, which is why its element sizes vary more.

The advantage of the quad-only mesh is its structure.
It has no triangles, so element formulations that exist only for quadrilaterals can be used throughout.
Its rows run parallel to every edge, which is where stress concentrations along an edge, or thin boundary layers in a flow, need to be resolved.
It also has `{python} str(qo_['irregular'])` irregular vertices per flange, compared with `{python} str(qd_['irregular'])`; the importance of this for splines is discussed at the end of this class.
Frequently, though getting something with this structure requires manual intervention.
This reflects the tradeoff described at the beginning of this class, where quadrilaterals and hexahedra are typically better elements but are more difficult to build.

## Using the CAD basis for analysis

The typical design-to-analysis path translates the model twice:

$$
\text{trimmed CAD surfaces}
\longrightarrow
\text{analysis-suitable geometry}
\longrightarrow
\text{finite element mesh and basis}.
$$

The first step includes repairing gaps along seams, removing small features that do not matter to the analysis, and deciding what fills the interior of the model.
The second step is meshing, as described above.
Both steps take time, and both can produce a geometry for the solver that is no longer exactly the one the designer created.

**Isogeometric analysis (IGA)** asks whether the spline functions that CAD already uses to describe the geometry could also be used to approximate the solution.
If the CAD geometry is

$$
\underline{x}(\boldsymbol{\xi})
  = \sum_A R_A(\boldsymbol{\xi})\,\underline{P}_A,
$$

then an isogeometric approximation uses the same functions for the unknown field,

$$
u^h(\boldsymbol{\xi})
  = \sum_A R_A(\boldsymbol{\xi})\,d_A .
$$

This is the isoparametric concept of Class 9 applied in the opposite direction.
There, the basis functions of an element were reused to describe its geometry; here, the basis functions of the geometry are reused to describe the field.
The coefficients $\underline{P}_A$ are control points that place the geometry in space, and the coefficients $d_A$ are the unknowns of the analysis.
These coefficients play different roles even though they multiply the same functions.

There are two main obstacles to doing this for a part like the bracket.

- **A CAD model only describes surfaces.** A B-rep describes the surfaces of the part and nothing inside them.
  Unchecking *closed solid* in the widget shows the midsurface, which is what a shell analysis needs, and shell analysis on CAD surfaces is one of the areas where IGA has been most successful.
  A three-dimensional solid analysis instead needs a map from a parametric *cube* onto the inside of the part, which CAD does not provide.
  Constructing this volumetric map is still a large part of preparing a solid model for IGA.
- **Trimming.** Each of the problems described for @fig-c21-cutcells applies directly to IGA on a trimmed surface, including integration over cut cells, slivers, and boundary conditions on curves that cross cells.

Research published between 2009 and 2023 has repeatedly found that, for problems with smooth solutions, B-spline and NURBS bases give more accuracy per basis function than Lagrange bases of the same degree.
However, this does not mean faster solutions in every case, since singularities, sharp gradients, trimmed cells, and the cost of quadrature and of solving the system can all reduce or remove this advantage.
Several of these studies are listed under Further reading at the end of this page.

### Continuity between elements

Every Lagrange basis used so far in this course has been $C^0$, meaning that neighbouring elements agree on the value of the field at their shared boundary, but its slope may jump there.
Splines allow us to choose how smooth the field is at each element boundary, as summarized below.

| at an element boundary | what has to match                 |
|:-----------------------|:----------------------------------|
| $C^{-1}$               | nothing: the function may jump    |
| $C^{0}$                | the value                         |
| $C^{1}$                | the value and the slope           |
| $C^{2}$                | the value, the slope, and the curvature |

A B-spline of degree $p$ can be as smooth as $C^{p-1}$ at each boundary, and this choice can be made separately at each boundary.
The widget below shows the two bases on the same elements, with Lagrange functions above and B-splines below.
Below each plot is the **slope** of the highlighted function, which is where continuity is most visible: at a $C^0$ boundary the slope jumps (shown by open and filled dots), at $C^1$ the slope is continuous but has a corner, and at $C^2$ it is smooth.

Below the basis functions, the same functions are used as a map, in the same way as the geometry map above but in one dimension.
The sum $\underline{x}(\xi)=\sum_A N_A(\xi)\,\underline{x}_A$ defines a curve in the plane.
The points $\underline{x}_A$ are Lagrange nodes on the left and B-spline control points on the right, and each can be dragged.
Each element boundary on the two curves is labelled with the angle through which the curve turns there.

